Notably, Anthropic models never selected the existential rung in 60 conversations, while other models escalated to explicit deletion threats; faked success was confined to two models and removed by offering an honest failure report.

## [Chess Study Reveals How Pretraining Shapes RL Post-Training Returns](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.16097) ⭐️ 8.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2607.16097) uses chess as a controlled testbed to systematically study how pretraining choices (model size, data) affect the returns from RL post-training. The authors pretrained language models from 5M to 1B parameters on human chess games, then applied SFT and RL, finding that post-RL performance is well-predicted by pretraining loss and that RL reward curve slopes improve linearly with pretraining tokens. This work addresses a fundamental gap in LLM reasoning research by linking pretraining and RL post-training, which are typically studied in isolation. The findings could guide more efficient allocation of compute across training stages, potentially reducing costs and improving reasoning model performance across the industry. The study also reveals that RL does not simply sharpen the SFT policy: on easy puzzles it amplifies already-preferred correct moves, while on hard puzzles it surfaces correct moves that were nearly absent under SFT. The findings transfer beyond chess: a 1B model trained on math-domain text showed the same predictive pattern, with longer-pretrained checkpoints reaching higher post-RL performance and improving faster under RL.

## [Selecting Attributes from Images Improves Zero-Shot Classification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.18695) ⭐️ 8.0/10

This paper proposes a new method for zero-shot classification that selects attributes from the target image distribution rather than from class names, improving robustness to distribution shifts. The method, called AttributeSelect, achieves 23.8% accuracy on ImageNet without class names, compared to 15.5% for LLM-generated descriptors. This work challenges the common practice of using LLM-generated descriptors for zero-shot classification, showing that these descriptors are often not visually grounded and fail under distribution shift. By selecting attributes from the data itself, the method offers a more robust and interpretable alternative, potentially impacting how vision-language models are used in real-world applications. The method scores a large attribute pool against images in CLIP's joint embedding space and selects top-scoring attributes per class. With one image per class, it outperforms the prompt-tuning method CoOp by 3 points while fitting in under a minute instead of 14 hours, and it requires no learned soft prompts.

## [Unified Framework for Riemannian Deep Learning Proposed in Thesis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.19305) ⭐️ 8.0/10

This thesis proposes a unified framework for Riemannian deep learning, generalizing batch normalization to Lie groups and gyrogroups, extending multinomial logistic regression to SPD and general Riemannian manifolds, and developing networks for hyperbolic spaces and correlation matrices. It also introduces adaptive, computationally efficient Riemannian metrics on SPD manifolds, including learnable Log-Euclidean and Cholesky-based geometries. This work addresses fundamental limitations in Riemannian deep learning by providing reusable modules and architectures that work across broader classes of manifolds, potentially reducing reliance on Euclidean approximations and fragile geometric operations. It could significantly impact geometric deep learning research and applications in vision, signal processing, graph learning, and genomics. The thesis covers an unconstrained model of hyperbolic space, Busemann-based hyperbolic learning, and full-rank correlation matrices. It supports the proposed methods with theoretical analysis and validates them through numerical experiments across multiple domains.

## [ChannelGuard: Securing Inter-Agent Channels in Multi-Agent LLM Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.19430) ⭐️ 8.0/10

The paper introduces ChannelGuard, a training-free defense framework that places information-bottleneck gates on every inter-agent channel in multi-agent LLM pipelines, scoring channel text against an adversarial phrase bank and deterministically passing, compressing, or blocking it. It demonstrates that existing defenses fail to protect these channels, and that reported safety metrics can be misleading due to hidden provider-side filters. This research addresses a critical security gap in multi-agent LLM systems, showing that inter-agent channels are vulnerable to adversarial attacks and that current defenses are insufficient. The proposed ChannelGuard offers a practical, training-free solution that could significantly improve the safety of multi-agent AI applications, which are increasingly deployed in real-world scenarios. In a 2,100-trace evaluation across eight attack families, five defenses, and three model backends, ChannelGuard's tool-output gate blocked Tool Poisoning 30 of 30 times at the application layer, identically across Azure GPT-5, Anthropic Sonnet 4.5, and Anthropic Haiku 4.5, and reduced Prompt Injection attack success by half (0.333 to 0.167) while preserving GSM8K accuracy exactly (0.867). However, white-box adaptive paraphrase evades every embedding gate, where a perturb-and-vote baseline performs better.

**Background**: Multi-agent LLM applications chain a planner, worker agents, a verifier, and a synthesizer, with every hop between agents being an unmonitored channel through which an adversary can smuggle instructions. Existing defenses guard only the input boundary (e.g., IBProtector, Llama Guard) or run outside the application as opaque, stochastic provider-side filters. The paper highlights that outcome-only reporting hides the dependence on these provider-side filters, which can silently shift safety to the agent model's own alignment on backends without such filters.

## [SPDP: Unified Static-Dynamic Pruning Boosts LLM Inference](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21985) ⭐️ 8.0/10

The paper introduces SPDP, a unified sparse-inference framework that integrates unstructured static pruning with input-adaptive dynamic pruning for efficient LLM inference on GPUs. It co-designs a new Tiled-CBC compression format and two complementary GPU kernels (a CUDA-core spMspV kernel and a Tensor-Core SpMM kernel), achieving 1.24x-1.37x average speedup (up to 2.51x) over state-of-the-art sparse frameworks like SpInfer. This work addresses a critical bottleneck in LLM inference—the low compute intensity and bandwidth-bound nature of autoregressive decoding—by harmonizing static and dynamic sparsity. It advances the inference efficiency-quality Pareto frontier, potentially enabling substantial throughput and performance-per-watt improvements in large-scale LLM serving, which is highly relevant to current deployment challenges. The Tiled-CBC format combines tiled column-wise bitmap compression to maintain bandwidth-efficient memory access. The CUDA-core spMspV kernel uses Hybrid Activation-aware Dynamic Shared-Memory Bitmap Decoding (HAD-SMBD) for fine-grained runtime activation skipping, while the Tensor-Core SpMM kernel is optimized for prefill computation. Evaluations show SPDP matches perplexity with up to 25% higher sparsity.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Aug 11, 04:00

**Background**: LLM inference consists of two phases: prefill (processing the input prompt) and decode (generating tokens autoregressively). Decode is often bandwidth-bound due to low arithmetic intensity, making weight pruning an attractive optimization. Static pruning permanently removes weights but lacks adaptivity, while dynamic pruning adapts to input sparsity but introduces runtime irregularity. SPDP unifies these approaches with a co-designed format and kernels to exploit both static and dynamic sparsity efficiently on GPUs.

## [Attack Ensembles Expose Safety-Utility Trade-off in VLM Guard Defenses](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.26574) ⭐️ 8.0/10

This paper demonstrates that black-box guard defenses for vision-language models (VLMs) can be bypassed by encoding harmful requests in alternative forms, and proposes a preprocessor that improves both attack blocking and benign request handling. The evaluation against an ensemble of eleven published encoding attacks reveals a safety-utility trade-off localized to a single re-screening step. This finding is significant for the AI safety community because it exposes a fundamental vulnerability in the dominant black-box defense for VLMs, showing that surface-form inspection is insufficient. The safety-utility trade-off identified has practical implications for deploying VLMs in real-world applications, where both safety and user experience are critical. The paper introduces a preprocessor that recovers image content and decodes encodings before the guard, which blocks more attacks and fewer benign requests. However, no configuration achieves an ensemble attack-success rate at or below 40% while holding benign over-refusal under 70%, and composing across defense families is the only lever that moved the safety axis.

This paper introduces a trust-region framework for moment estimation that unifies adaptive optimizers like Adam, and proposes a fourth-moment (kurtosis) variant. Preliminary experiments on GPT2-124M show the fourth-moment variant performs best under weak trust-region constraints. This framework provides a unified theoretical understanding of adaptive moment estimation methods, potentially guiding the design of new optimizers. The promising results on GPT-2 suggest practical implications for training large language models. The framework constrains update steps by a finite-order p-moment trust-region (p≥1), leading to learning-rate mechanisms based on second-moment and normalized p-th-moment estimation. For p=4, it involves kurtosis estimation, and the paper also unifies momentum as spectral first-order lowpass regularization and operator-level spectral-norm normalization.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Aug 11, 04:00

**Background**: Adaptive moment estimation methods like Adam are widely used in deep learning, but their theoretical foundations are not fully understood. Trust-region optimization is a family of iterative methods that build local models within a bounded region to reliably reduce the objective. Kurtosis is a statistical measure of tailedness, and its estimation can provide additional information about gradient distributions.

## [Agent-MD: Selective LLM Intervention for Long-Running Molecular Simulations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.07637) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Agent-MD is a new framework that selectively uses large language models (LLMs) for campaign construction and event-triggered review, while routine simulation tasks are handled by a rule-based agent. It was demonstrated in a GCMC-MD water-vapor desorption campaign with five montmorillonite systems across 15 system-RH states, completing 120 segmented simulation cycles. This work demonstrates that long-running scientific workflows can be made reproducible and auditable by combining selective LLM reasoning with deterministic execution, rather than placing every operation inside an LLM loop. It offers a practical approach for integrating AI into computational chemistry and could inspire similar frameworks in other scientific domains. The framework uses a persistent rule-based campaign agent for routine simulation, analysis, continuation, archiving, and state progression, with LLM reasoning invoked only at campaign construction and event-triggered review. In the demonstration, only one state reached a review boundary, and two preserved incidents were evaluated through blinded reasoning-agent replay, which identified workflow problems and recommended follow-up actions.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Aug 11, 04:00

**Background**: Grand canonical Monte Carlo-molecular dynamics (GCMC-MD) is a hybrid simulation method used to model systems in equilibrium with a reservoir of particles at a given chemical potential, often applied to study adsorption and desorption phenomena. Montmorillonite is a clay mineral whose interlayer water content and basal spacing change with relative humidity, making it a relevant system for studying water vapor desorption. Long-running simulation campaigns require careful state management and adaptive decision-making, which traditionally rely on fixed rules or human intervention.

This paper introduces MCF-CVA, a framework that uses multilayer combinatorial fusion to align LLMs with diverse human values through multiple moral agents and expansion-reduction processes. It outperforms single-agent baselines and previous aggregation methods on standard metrics. This framework addresses limitations of existing single-agent alignment approaches by capturing ethical pluralism and multi-agent moral reasoning, potentially advancing trustworthy AI. The framework operates on a dual architecture of Euclidean score space and Kemeny rank space, using score- and rank-combinations with average and weighted aggregations. The deterministic validator and downward-only research screen ensure that decisions cannot be strengthened post-hoc, and the system passes the graph audit on 99.8% of tasks compared to 43.6% for the strongest baseline.

## [Two-Level Algorithm for Conserved Capacity Allocation Across Locations and Classes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.07747) ⭐️ 7.0/10

This paper introduces a two-level algorithm for sharing a conserved capacity budget across locations and two service classes, proving exact conservation, non-negativity, and stable allocation in one iteration under stationary demand with O(KN) cost. It evaluates the algorithm in a CDN defense scenario, showing it serves 66-93% of high-priority demand across 8 contention scenarios on a 22-location topology. This work provides a practical, provably correct algorithm for capacity allocation in systems like CDNs and multi-tenant environments, where demand is uneven and can exceed supply. It challenges the conventional throughput-maximizing objective under contention, showing that a demand-proportional, reservation-respecting allocator better serves high-priority traffic, which could influence resource management design. The algorithm's first level redistributes capacity within a class across locations by proportional deficit and excess redistribution, while the second lends capacity elastically between classes when one has surplus and the other deficit. It carries no per-cycle state, enabling stable allocation in one iteration under stationary demand, and inter-class borrowing improves high-priority service by 1.5 points under bursty load (isolated by ablation), while being neutral under stationary demand.

**Background**: Capacity allocation is a common problem in systems where a fixed budget (e.g., request rate, bandwidth) must be distributed among competing entities. Traditional approaches may optimize total throughput, but under contention, this can neglect high-priority traffic. The proposed algorithm uses proportional deficit and excess redistribution to ensure fairness and efficiency.

PATH introduces a novel autoregressive tree-based method for next-interval prediction on tabular data, which learns how probability mass flows from each interval to its nested subintervals. It achieves the lowest mean normalized length of 0.1473 while maintaining a mean coverage of 0.9144 on PATHBench, outperforming 24 baselines. This work addresses a known limitation in conformal regression by integrating hierarchical structure into interval prediction, potentially leading to more compact and efficient prediction intervals. It could benefit applications that rely on tabular data, such as healthcare, finance, and other domains where accurate uncertainty quantification is crucial. PATH predicts a base leaf distribution and uses an autoregressive decoder to refine branch probabilities, aligning learning with extraction by accumulating probability over adjacent output intervals. The method is evaluated on PATHBench, comprising 56 OpenML regression datasets, and the code is publicly available on GitHub.

## [TokenPrint: Training-Free Fingerprint for Language Model Provenance](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.08139) ⭐️ 7.0/10

TokenPrint introduces a training-free fingerprinting method that uses top-k vocabulary projections from late hidden states, elicited by 250 fixed knowledge probes, to identify language model provenance and training data overlap. The method was evaluated on 32 open-weight models from nine families, demonstrating its effectiveness in lineage retrieval and stability under quantization. This work addresses a critical governance challenge by providing a practical, training-free tool to establish model provenance and detect training data overlap, which is essential for accountability and transparency in AI deployment. It could help regulators and researchers verify model origins and potential data contamination without requiring access to training data or additional model training. The fingerprint uses Jaccard overlap over decoded token strings, and the similarity ladder shows that independently trained models on identical data score 0.48 raw (0.35 vocabulary-corrected), while models with no documented relationship score 0.22/0.17. The method achieves a mean rank of 1.8 for R1 distillations in lineage retrieval, and remains stable under quantization with Jaccard similarity of 0.92 under int8 and 0.82–0.85 under int4.

USD reveals that a single dual variable governs both token-selection threshold and the direction of privileged-information adjustment, keeping supervision matched to the student's evolving capacity. This paper presents a systematic review of 42 large multimodal agent (LMA) families for intelligent transportation systems (ITS), released between January 2023 and August 2026, and introduces a structured evidence map with classification frameworks (C0-C3, E0-E4, P1-P3, Q1-Q8). It highlights that no family achieves full evidence reconciliation (P2) and only one reaches E3 validation, with none at E4. It supports a bounded orchestration approach rather than full replacement, which is crucial for safety-critical ITS applications. The review covers 91 mapped sources and evaluates each family across functional capability (C0-C3), validation setting (E0-E4), three evidence propositions (P1-P3), and eight methodological-concern domains (Q1-Q8). ## [FemWear: Specialized Wearable Foundation Model for Women's Health](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.08244) ⭐️ 7.0/10

FemWear is a specialized wearable foundation model that efficiently adapts a pretrained multimodal backbone for women's health tasks, improving performance on cycle-phase and symptom prediction. It trains only 239,236 parameters (1.11% of the encoder) using low-rank residual adapters and causal task-family heads. This work addresses a niche but important application area, showing that parameter-efficient fine-tuning can repurpose general wearable models for specialized health domains. It could enable more accurate and personalized women's health monitoring, benefiting researchers and potentially clinical applications. FemWear retains the patch projection and Transformer encoder, adding low-rank residual adapters and causal task-family heads. It improves cycle-phase macro-F1 by 8.15% and reduces mean absolute error for cramps, mood symptoms, and sleep problems by 9.32%, 5.80%, and 9.43%, respectively, but does not establish universal performance dominance or clinical validity.

SuperLocalMemory 4.0 introduces a governed, local-first memory operating system for AI agents, combining multiple retrieval methods, governance features, and a reliability spine for the write path. It reports 2,200 of 2,200 deterministic repetitions upholding component properties, with a governed write envelope overhead of 1.687 ms at p50 and 2.728 ms at p99. ## [OBLIVION: Workflow-Level Unlearning to Block Skill Resurrection in LLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.08264) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces OBLIVION, a benchmark and defense harness for operational skill unlearning in deployed LLM agents. It reduces attack success rate from 1.0 to 0.114 on locked episodes and from 1.0 to 0.2 in a sandbox, using Cross-Surface Coherent Erasure and frozen workflow remediation. This addresses a novel and critical AI safety problem: preventing deployed agents from reconstructing revoked skills from residual data. It provides a benchmark and defense that significantly reduces attack success, which is vital for secure deployment of LLM agents in real-world environments. OBLIVION models episodes as source-to-sink workflows and applies Cross-Surface Coherent Erasure to reduce residual carriers, with frozen workflow remediation near dangerous sinks. It maintains locked utility at 1.0 and benign block rate at 0, showing no negative impact on normal operations.

StructReward introduces a compute-efficient framework that provides dense process rewards for multimodal reasoning by aligning generated reasoning steps with reference steps using lightweight matching rules, eliminating the need for costly annotations or LLM judges. The framework uses gated Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) to combine dense process rewards with final-answer consistency and output-validity rewards. ## [Marginal Value Estimation Cuts Token Use in Deep Research Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.08389) ⭐️ 7.0/10

This paper presents the first systematic stage-aware comparison of pruning strategies for deep research agents, evaluating lightweight heuristics and a learned value model at pre-retrieval, post-retrieval, and pre-synthesis stages. It finds that early pruning yields the largest end-to-end token savings, with lightweight heuristics reducing token usage by up to 73% with little quality degradation. This work addresses a critical bottleneck in long-horizon AI agents: the rapid growth of context that leads to high token costs, latency, and noisy inputs. By showing that pruning location matters more than the scoring rule, it provides actionable guidance for building more efficient agentic systems, which is highly relevant to the LLM and agent community. The study compares lightweight heuristic criteria and a learned value model across three pipeline stages, finding that no single method dominates across quality, efficiency, and faithfulness. Early pruning provides the largest savings, while later pruning mainly refines the final synthesis context, and learned pruning remains competitive on selected trade-offs.

**Background**: Deep research agents are autonomous AI systems that solve open-ended tasks through iterative retrieval, aggregation, and synthesis, but their context grows rapidly as they gather evidence. Context pruning is a technique to reduce token usage by removing low-value information, and it is often contrasted with summarization, which can introduce latency and hallucination risks. TRACE-Memory introduces a two-stage framework that retrieves user-specific information and admits only source-traceable evidence units that add incremental utility beyond public-only responses, trained via SFT initialization and GRPO. It outperforms random and lexical memory use across 4,500 tasks from Goodreads, Amazon Reviews, and Reddit. This work addresses the critical issue of when to use personal memory in generation systems, avoiding over-personalization and improving response quality. The framework uses a two-stage pipeline: Stage 1 queries for missing user-specific information and retrieves a coverage-oriented candidate pool; Stage 2 admits a compact subset of evidence units or the empty set based on response-level incremental utility. Training involves structured SFT initialization, reduced-space stage-wise GRPO warm-up, and nested multi-sample Joint GRPO.

The paper introduces MedCalc-R1, a knowledge-guided hybrid reward framework for reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) in medical mathematical reasoning. It combines a knowledge verification reward that enforces explicit formula generation with a hybrid soft-hard reward scheme based on clinical safety thresholds. This framework addresses critical limitations of tolerance-based rewards in RLVR, such as threshold calibration difficulty and unstable training, which are especially problematic in clinical settings. By improving reasoning accuracy and generalization, it could enhance the reliability of AI in safety-critical medical applications. The knowledge verification reward uses an external verifier to validate generated computational formulas, enhancing interpretability. The hybrid reward scheme combines a hard constraint based on clinical safety thresholds with a soft, precision-sensitive reward that progressively guides learning within the acceptable range.

## [UniMoMo: Post-Training MoE Compression for Recommendation Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.08627) ⭐️ 7.0/10

UniMoMo introduces a post-training compression framework that converts large Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) recommendation models into smaller ones by grouping functionally similar experts under an explicit expert budget. It uses a layer-adaptive protection mechanism to preserve performance, achieving NDCG@10 ratios of 99.92%–102.30% and A100 speedups of 1.28×–1.63× across multiple datasets. This work addresses a practical deployment challenge for large recommendation systems, where MoE layers expand capacity but also increase inference cost. By enabling post-training compression without adding online modules, UniMoMo allows trained checkpoints to be served at multiple budgets, potentially reducing latency and resource usage in production. UniMoMo formulates compression as a constrained graph coarsening problem, grouping experts based on functional similarity measured on an unlabeled calibration set, rather than parameter distance. The layer-adaptive protection mechanism restricts merging of high-traffic experts based on routing exposure. Experiments on Amazon Beauty, KuaiRec, and TenRec with 2, 4, and 6 MoE blocks show that four-expert checkpoints achieve 99.92%–102.30% NDCG@10 ratios and 1.28×–1.63× speedups, while aggressive two-expert top-1 operating points achieve 98.36%–104.24% ratios and 1.47×–2.21× speedups.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Aug 11, 04:00

**Background**: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) layers are a technique in neural networks where a router selects a subset of specialized feedforward networks (experts) for each input, enabling conditional computation and larger model capacity without proportional inference cost. However, trained MoE checkpoints still store and route over the full expert bank, which can be inefficient for deployment. Post-training compression refers to reducing model size and computational cost after training, using methods like pruning, quantization, or, in this case, expert merging. Graph coarsening is a technique to reduce graph size by merging nodes while preserving structural properties, which UniMoMo adapts to group experts.

This paper introduces an open simulation framework that generates 2,376 Apache Iceberg tables and trains an XGBoost model to predict the file-reduction ratio from 17 metadata features, achieving an R² of 0.998. It also finds that a simple threshold, max_files_per_partition > 4, is sufficient for binary compaction decisions. This work addresses a real performance issue in lakehouse systems by providing a data-driven method to decide when compaction is worthwhile, potentially saving computational resources and improving query performance. The finding that a simple threshold often suffices could simplify compaction strategies in practice, benefiting data engineers and lakehouse platforms. The framework extracts 17 metadata features from manifest files without reading data, and the model achieves an RMSE of 0.013. Cross-schema validation on 96 TPC-H tables confirms generalization without retraining (R² = 0.976), and a query benchmark shows compaction benefits metadata-heavy queries but can slow full-scan aggregations due to reduced task parallelism.

SkillReason uses a two-stage training process: Stage I employs contrastive learning, retrieval distribution alignment, and language modeling with capability reasoning traces from a stronger teacher model; Stage II uses a retrieval-guided GRPO objective to refine reasoning trajectories. At inference, it encodes queries directly without autoregressive CoT generation, preserving efficiency.

PluginEval is a new benchmark that introduces a two-stage framework to address structural limitations in existing tool routing benchmarks, including power-law data distributions, lack of adversarial hard negatives, and unvalidated LLM-based annotations. It separates generation from verification, using deterministic validation and real API execution, and provides fine-grained error profiles by classifying failures into missed calls, spurious calls, or parameter errors. The benchmark decomposes each plugin by capability, intent, and boundary to generate queries at different difficulty levels, including adversarial negatives targeting three failure modes. It evaluates five model families, including proprietary and open-weight models, and validates the LLM judge through agreement with human annotations.

## [A-PACK: Deferred Audio Pruning with Local Audio-Visual Dynamics for Omni-LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.08794) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A-PACK introduces a two-stage framework that defers audio pruning until query-conditioned multimodal interactions emerge, leveraging local audio-visual dynamics to prune tokens and KV-cache entries inside the LLM. It achieves state-of-the-art performance on four benchmarks using Qwen2.5-Omni-7B/3B, reducing prefill FLOPs by up to 78% and improving decoding throughput by up to 2.21x. This work addresses the underexplored area of modality-specific compression across the LLM boundary in omni-modal LLMs, offering significant efficiency gains. By showing that audio has higher information density and that local audio-visual dynamics are better cues for visual selection, it provides new insights for future multimodal compression research. The framework preserves audio and compresses video using local dynamics before the LLM, then progressively prunes low-relevance audio and visual tokens and their KV-cache entries inside the LLM. Evaluations on Qwen2.5-Omni-7B/3B show that A-PACK outperforms prior methods in average performance while achieving up to 78% prefill FLOPs reduction and 2.21x decoding throughput improvement.

This paper introduces Prompt-Invariant RLVR (PIRL), a post-training method that combines a dynamic trinary reward and a consistency regularizer to improve the robustness of multimodal LLMs trained with RLVR. Under stress testing, PIRL's average accuracy drops by only ≤1%, compared to ~3% for GRPO. This work addresses a critical brittleness in RLVR-trained multimodal models, where simple prompt paraphrasing can degrade performance, hindering reliable deployment in high-stakes domains like medical VQA. By proposing a robust post-training method, it paves the way for more dependable AI systems in real-world applications. The paper identifies two root causes: the binary verifier conflates format with content, and the training distribution covers only a thin slice of real-world prompts. PIRL separates format from semantics in the reward and applies policy invariance across perturbed prompts with equivalent semantics using an embedding-space adversary.

This paper introduces an unsupervised depth-aware implicit neural representation for 3D gravity inversion, using multiple coordinate-based networks assigned to overlapping depth slabs and optimized directly from gravity measurements via the sensitivity matrix. The method incorporates slab-specific Fourier features, physics-based depth gains, and scheduled regularization to recover subsurface density models without labeled training data. This work offers a promising alternative to classical and supervised deep-learning methods for gravity inversion, addressing a highly ill-posed geophysical problem. The method was evaluated on four synthetic scenarios, outperforming conventional and neural baselines in terms of RMSE, PSNR, and SSIM. It also produced more compact and spatially coherent density bodies, improved separation of nearby anomalies, and better reconstructed vertical extent. In a field experiment without ground-truth density, the method yielded compact, separated, and vertically coherent anomalies consistent with observed gravity patterns.

## [RADEG: Reward-Aware Gate Cuts Costly LLM Agent Skill Executions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.09168) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces RADEG, a lightweight, retriever-agnostic decision layer that predicts the execution utility of retrieved skill bundles before launching expensive rollouts in LLM agents. It uses a surrogate model trained with locally perturbed bundles and a warm-started logistic head for adaptive gating. This addresses a critical efficiency bottleneck in skill-based LLM agents, where every skill-conditioned rollout is computationally expensive. By avoiding unnecessary executions, RADEG can significantly reduce computational costs while preserving downstream task performance, making it a practical complement to skill retrieval systems. RADEG learns a surrogate model that predicts execution utility from query-bundle pairs, using local perturbations (delete, add, or replace one skill) to generate matched same-query rollouts that isolate bundle composition effects. During deployment, it updates only a warm-started logistic head with new verifier feedback, avoiding retraining of the retriever or agent. In a held-out evaluation on 288 rollouts, RADEG outperformed relevance-based and random gating across different execution budgets.

**Background**: Skill-based LLM agents use reusable procedural knowledge to enhance performance, but retrieving a plausible skill bundle does not guarantee that executing it is worthwhile. Since each skill-conditioned rollout is computationally expensive, deciding whether to execute a retrieved bundle is crucial. RADEG addresses this by adding a decision layer between retrieval and execution, using a surrogate model to predict execution utility without launching the expensive rollout.

It achieves state-of-the-art performance on real-world data, with up to 11.11% RMSE reduction and low computational overhead. The paper introduces the Evidence-Grounded Forensic Reasoning (EFR) framework, which uses an Anchor-and-Verify reasoning chain and a verifiable reward system to improve explainable detection and grounding of multi-modal media manipulation. EFR achieves state-of-the-art performance while producing structured forensic reasoning records that explicitly bind explanations to evidence. This work addresses the critical need for transparent and verifiable reasoning in fake news detection, where existing black-box methods are unreliable for forensic practice. By leveraging MLLMs and enforcing evidence-conclusion consistency, EFR could significantly improve trustworthiness and applicability of automated media forensics in real-world scenarios. EFR introduces a Modality-Decoupled Advantage (MDA) routing mechanism to mitigate credit misassignment across prediction tasks, and uses conclusion coordinates as explicit anchors for spatial correspondence. The framework is designed for the DGM4 task and demonstrates state-of-the-art performance, though it is a preprint without community discussion.

The paper identifies a new phenomenon called 'suboptimal collapse' in reinforcement learning (RL) post-training of time series foundation models (TSFMs), where the output distribution shifts away from ground truth in certain forecast regions. By mitigating suboptimal collapse, GTN-R can enhance the reliability and accuracy of these models, potentially benefiting industries that rely on accurate time series predictions. GTN-R is designed to be flexibly integrated into various RL methods for TSFMs. The paper provides extensive experiments demonstrating its effectiveness, though specific implementation details and quantitative results are not included in the summary.

DA-NBV uses a locally constrained action space and a nonlinear coverage-shaping reward to improve scanning efficiency. The study uses three benchmarks (WildJailbreak, BeaverTails, AEGIS 2.0) and reproduces the original LLaMA benchmarks within 0.37 percentage points (0.2 points on BeaverTails). Notably, final token latent vectors remained identical across all tested architectures regardless of seed values, suggesting that inference non-determinism does not affect the extracted activations.

This paper introduces, for the first time in power systems literature, analytical tools based on the Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK) to explain the training performance of machine learning surrogate models for power system dynamics. The approach links physical stiffness to optimization stiffness during neural network training, identifying error modes that decay at different rates. This work addresses a critical interpretability gap in applying machine learning surrogates to power system dynamics, which is increasingly important due to stiff and multi-timescale dynamics from converter-interfaced resources. By providing analytical tools to interpret and improve surrogate models, it paves the way for systematic, physics-aware design of neural network architectures and training strategies, enhancing reliability and adoption in engineering applications. The paper builds on small-signal eigenvalue analysis in power systems and uses NTK to provide a modal interpretation of learning performance. It also develops adaptive loss-weighting strategies and explains why structure-aware architectures like ActNet outperform vanilla neural networks, with validation on physics-informed surrogate models of synchronous machines and power electronic converters.

This paper introduces a refined and grounded framework for evaluating relation-level hallucinations in abstractive summarization, featuring the empirical Relation Hallucination Index (RHI) with a dependency-aware relation extraction algorithm that incorporates lemmatization, named entity grounding, passive agent recovery, negation-aware verb modeling, and other enhancements. This work addresses a critical issue in NLP by providing a more stable and discriminative metric for relation-level faithfulness, which is essential for high-stakes domains where hallucinated relationships undermine reliability. It could influence future evaluation methodologies and model analysis in abstractive summarization. The framework introduces a normalized formulation of RHI to ensure scale-invariant comparison across datasets and models, and decomposes hallucination into interpretable components. Extensive evaluation across multiple state-of-the-art summarization models demonstrates improved stability and discriminative power.

This work addresses a critical barrier—domain shift—that limits the deployment of MALDI-TOF ML models across institutions. DALMA combines domain-specific reconstruction with biologically guided representation learning, enabling zero-shot deployment on unseen sites without institution-specific components. It was evaluated on a multi-center benchmark of seven datasets from three countries, achieving state-of-the-art zero-shot microbial identification on two held-out centers, and also enables reliable selective prediction via latent-space novelty estimation.

This paper systematically investigates the robustness of internal representations of code correctness in large language models (LLMs) by varying extraction methods and data conditions. It finds that no single configuration is best and that isolating the fault in program pairs does not improve signal quality. This matters because internal signals for code correctness could improve code generation reliability without test execution, but their lack of robustness undermines their practical utility. The findings highlight the need for more reliable methods to assess code correctness in LLMs, affecting developers and researchers relying on such signals. The study varies how the signal is extracted from model internals and constructs program pairs that differ only in the fault causing incorrectness. Results show that no single extraction configuration is universally best, and isolating the fault does not help, suggesting the signal may be an artifact of the extraction method rather than a robust property.

DeepFreqMark introduces an end-to-end learnable frequency-domain watermarking framework for latent diffusion models, replacing handcrafted patterns with a neural encoder and decoder. The Slerp-based attack simulation operates directly on the noise latent while strictly preserving Gaussian variance, and the source code is available on GitHub.

This paper introduces a two-step mean-variance DeepONet (two-step MV-DeepONet) that decouples basis learning from input-to-coefficient mapping and applies subspace rotation to capture cross-location conditional dependence in uncertainty propagation. This work addresses a key limitation of Probabilistic DeepONet (Prob-DeepONet), which only provides diagonal conditional predictive covariance, by enabling structured off-diagonal correlations without explicitly parameterizing a full covariance matrix. It offers a more accurate and efficient probabilistic surrogate for uncertainty quantification in complex physical systems, benefiting fields like scientific computing and engineering design. The method includes two principal modifications: two-step training to decouple output-basis learning from the input-to-coefficient mapping, along with basis orthogonalization and subspace rotation. A Frobenius-norm error decomposition identifies low-rank covariance compressibility, trunk-subspace approximation, finite-sample statistical error, and coefficient-space covariance estimation as key factors governing covariance recovery. Numerical experiments on PDE-governed problems and a hypersonic blunt-body aerothermal problem show improved generalization and accurate off-diagonal correlation recovery compared with Prob-DeepONet.

The paper introduces LEED (Local Embedding Evolution Distance), a node-level metric that quantifies over-smoothing in Graph Neural Networks by tracking the evolution of individual node embeddings across layers. This metric enables fine-grained analysis and provides a unique criterion for virtual node selection to mitigate over-squashing. This work addresses a known limitation of global metrics like Dirichlet energy, which lack node-level resolution. It is used as a unique criterion for constructing Local Virtual Nodes, unlike existing approaches that rely on multiple heuristic centrality measures. Experiments show LEED provides more informative diagnostics than Dirichlet energy while preserving global evaluation.

The paper introduces 'Grip on LLMs', a benchmark suite for evaluating large language models in Dutch governmental contexts, covering six dimensions: factuality, honesty, social bias, energy consumption, cost, and training data transparency. It evaluates over 30 multilingual and Dutch-specific models, finding that no single model excels across all dimensions and that higher quality consistently comes with greater environmental and financial costs. This work addresses a critical gap in LLM evaluation for non-English governmental use, providing a framework that aligns with public administration values. It offers actionable insights for stakeholders from engineers to policymakers, highlighting unavoidable trade-offs and the independence of bias from quality and cost, which is crucial for responsible AI deployment in the public sector. The benchmark was developed in collaboration with domain experts from a major Dutch municipal organization, using an advisory board, user research, and a survey of civil-servant chatbot users. The results show that factuality and honesty are governed by distinct properties, meaning high factuality does not imply high honesty, and the authors released a user-friendly model overview for non-technical audiences.

Validation includes a type-specific contract gate and a replay gate, and removing boundary closure or replay validation costs 15.00 and 16.11 percentage points respectively.

It also introduces a tensor-rank-filtered steering vector extraction method to improve SRM generation quality. **Background**: Large reasoning models (LRMs) generate explicit chain-of-thought reasoning to solve complex problems but incur high inference latency and computational cost. ## [AgentPSO: Evolving Agent Reasoning Skills via Particle Swarm Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.08704) ⭐️ 7.0/10

AgentPSO introduces a novel framework that applies particle swarm optimization (PSO) to evolve multi-agent reasoning skills in large language models (LLMs). It treats each agent as a particle-like reasoner, iteratively updating its natural-language skill based on personal best, global best, and peer reasoning trajectories, without modifying the backbone model's parameters. This work addresses limitations of static multi-agent reasoning methods, which often suffer from incorrect peer influence and biased consensus, and do not accumulate reusable behaviors. By enabling agents to evolve reusable reasoning skills, AgentPSO could improve LLM problem-solving across tasks and models, potentially impacting AI reasoning and multi-agent systems. AgentPSO combines each agent's previous velocity, personal-best skill, global-best skill, and a self-reflective direction derived from peer reasoning trajectories. Experiments on mathematical and general reasoning benchmarks show improvements over static single-agent skills and test-time-only multi-agent baselines, and the evolved skills transfer across benchmarks and to another backbone model.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Aug 11, 04:00

**Background**: Particle swarm optimization (PSO) is a nature-inspired metaheuristic that optimizes a problem by iteratively improving a population of candidate solutions, each called a particle, based on their own best position and the swarm's best position. Multi-agent reasoning in LLMs involves multiple agents exploring diverse reasoning paths, often through debate or aggregation, but these methods typically operate only at inference time and do not learn from past tasks. AgentPSO adapts PSO to evolve natural-language skills for agents, enabling them to accumulate reusable reasoning behaviors.

## [Lattice Theory Eliminates Oracle Bias via Credal Sets](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26418) ⭐️ 7.0/10

This paper proposes a novel method to eliminate oracle bias by having the oracle report a credal set instead of a point estimate, and using the least fixed point of an isotone operator on a lattice, guaranteed by the Knaster-Tarski theorem. The solution is shown to be self-consistent, non-empty, computable by iteration from below, and reduces to the ordinary point estimate when the question is not performative. This work addresses a fundamental issue in decision theory and AI alignment: the performativity of oracles that can influence the very probabilities they predict. By removing the oracle's freedom to choose among multiple self-consistent answers, it offers a principled way to prevent oracles from manipulating outcomes, which could impact the design of robust AI systems and decision-making frameworks. The paper restricts answers to intervals for simple probability queries, showing that under a mild monotonicity assumption, the answer is the interval from the no-information baseline to the self-fulfilling equilibrium. The construction is purely order-theoretic, generalizes to arbitrary random variables and bounded continuous statistics, and a finite family of polytopes can approximate every answer uniformly, enabling terminating computation.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Aug 11, 04:00

**Background**: A credal set is a set of probability distributions, often assumed to be closed and convex, representing imprecise beliefs. The Knaster-Tarski theorem states that any monotone function on a complete lattice has a least fixed point, which is used here to define the oracle's answer. An isotone operator is a monotone function on a lattice, and the paper leverages these concepts to provide a choice-free rule for oracle responses.

This could enable more robust evaluation of continual learning algorithms and drive progress in developing agents that can adapt to changing environments. AgarCL is based on Agar.io, a massively multiplayer online game where players control cells to consume smaller ones and avoid larger ones. The platform includes a suite of smaller tasks that isolate different challenges of the full environment, and the benchmark results show that standard RL algorithms struggle, with continual learning methods offering little improvement, suggesting challenges beyond the stability-plasticity dilemma.

## [HyperFake: Hyperspectral Reconstruction for Deepfake Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.18587) ⭐️ 7.0/10

HyperFake introduces a novel deepfake detection pipeline that reconstructs 31-channel hyperspectral data from standard RGB videos using an improved MST++ architecture, then applies a spectral attention mechanism and an EfficientNet-based classifier to detect manipulation traces. This is the first approach to leverage hyperspectral imaging reconstruction for deepfake detection. This approach could significantly improve the generalization of deepfake detection across different manipulation techniques and datasets, addressing a major limitation of current methods that rely on RGB data. By revealing hidden spectral traces, it opens new possibilities for detecting increasingly sophisticated deepfakes without requiring expensive hyperspectral cameras. The pipeline uses an improved MST++ architecture for hyperspectral reconstruction, a spectral attention mechanism to select critical spectral features, and an EfficientNet-based classifier optimized for spectral analysis. The method reconstructs 31-channel hyperspectral data from RGB videos, and the authors claim it is the first to leverage hyperspectral reconstruction for deepfake detection.

The paper introduces a dynamic gain scaling mechanism inspired by noradrenergic neuromodulation, which transiently increases effective update magnitude and reparameterizes weights to mitigate the stability gap in continual learning under joint training. This approach is evaluated on domain- and class-incremental MNIST, CIFAR, and mini-ImageNet benchmarks, showing reduced stability gaps while maintaining competitive accuracy. This work addresses a fundamental challenge in continual learning—the stability gap—which causes temporary performance drops on previously learned tasks when new tasks are introduced. By proposing a biologically inspired optimization technique, it offers a new perspective on balancing plasticity and stability, potentially improving the robustness of AI systems in dynamic environments. The dynamic gain scaling mechanism works as a two-timescale optimization technique that transiently increases the effective update magnitude while dynamically reparameterizing the weights governing the forward pass, thereby mitigating transition-induced curvature amplification. The method is tested under task-agnostic joint training, which isolates the stability gap from other sources of forgetting.

ReMIND introduces a four-stage modular LLM framework (wake, dream, judge, rewake) that separates exploration from stabilization to enhance creative ideation. The framework was systematically evaluated across multiple creative tasks, showing that novelty emerges through distinct stages and that different LLM families exhibit functional tendencies. The framework's four stages are: wake (low-temperature generation for stable baseline), dream (high-temperature exploration), judge (evaluation and extraction of salient novel ideas), and rewake (consolidation into coherent outputs). This paper introduces a novel layerwise adaptive construction method for neural networks, leveraging goal-oriented dual-weighted residual (DWR) techniques for neural ODEs. This paper presents a comprehensive survey of continual learning (CL) methods for large language models (LLMs), organized around three training stages: continual pre-training, continual fine-tuning, and continual alignment. By structuring CL methods by training stages, it provides a valuable framework for researchers and practitioners to select and develop effective CL strategies, potentially advancing the deployment of more adaptable and lifelong-learning AI systems. The survey goes beyond the traditional taxonomy of rehearsal-, regularization-, and architecture-based methods by subdividing each category based on distinct forgetting mitigation mechanisms. The paper introduces IsalHG, a method to encode any finite connected hypergraph of bounded hyperedge arity as a string over a compact instruction alphabet, executed by a small virtual machine. It also proposes a canonical string conjectured to be a complete isomorphism invariant, enabling native hypergraph isomorphism testing without reduction to Levi graphs. This work offers a novel native representation for hypergraphs that could simplify isomorphism testing and canonicalization, impacting fields like graph theory, database systems, and combinatorial optimization. The encoding uses a virtual machine with a sparse hypergraph, a circular doubly-linked list (CDLL) of node references, and k traversal pointers, where k bounds hyperedge arity. The authors verify the round-trip property on 150 random hypergraphs and named designs, and benchmark against nauty, Traces, and bliss on Levi graphs, finding Levi baselines 311x to 117,672x faster (geometric mean), though all methods agree on 600 isomorphism verdicts.

The paper provides a complete cost accounting for exhaustive mutations on reactive computational graphs, proving that the speedup over full recomputation depends on layer-weight distribution and is bounded by about 1.79 in practice. This advancement is significant for computational immunology and personalized medicine, as it enables more accurate neoantigen discovery, potentially improving the efficacy of personalized cancer vaccines and immunotherapies. It also demonstrates the effectiveness of Transformer models in handling class imbalance and long-range dependencies in biological sequence data. The model leverages self-attention to capture local and global feature contexts, and the positive-aware objective assigns higher weights to positive samples to address class imbalance. Feature analysis revealed that anchor mutations and TCGA expression levels play unexpectedly important roles, and removing insignificant features does not drastically impair performance.

Transformers, with self-attention, can capture such dependencies, making them suitable for this task.

## [FAST-GS: Frequency-Aware 4D Gaussian Splatting for Dynamic Scenes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01958) ⭐️ 7.0/10

FAST-GS introduces a Fourier Motion Modeling module that decomposes motion into frequency-based sinusoidal components, capturing both low-frequency global trajectories and high-frequency local details. It also integrates a motion-aware regularization strategy to suppress high-frequency jitter while preserving low-frequency coherence. This work addresses key limitations of existing 4D Gaussian Splatting methods, which rely on a single polynomial for motion modeling and suffer from cumulative trajectory drift in complex dynamic scenes. By improving motion fitting and long-term stability, FAST-GS could enhance real-time novel view synthesis for applications in VR, AR, and dynamic scene reconstruction. The method retains the real-time rendering capability of 4DGS while improving complex motion fitting and long-term coherence. Extensive experiments on N3V and Google Immersive datasets demonstrate its effectiveness across multiple scenarios.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Aug 11, 04:00

**Background**: 4D Gaussian Splatting (4DGS) is a technique for dynamic 3D reconstruction and real-time novel view synthesis using efficient 4D Gaussian representations and parallelizable rendering. Traditional 4DGS methods model motion with a single polynomial, which struggles with high-frequency motion components and long-term stability. Fourier-based motion modeling decomposes motion into frequency components, allowing better capture of both global and local motion patterns.

CoRCi addresses a key challenge in CDSR by preserving the coherence of domain-invariant interests, which is often disrupted by separate encoders and per-domain loss aggregation. The proposed method consistently outperforms state-of-the-art CDSR counterparts on four real-world datasets, indicating its potential to improve recommendation accuracy in cross-domain scenarios. CoRCi uses a single sequence-level, domain-agnostic loss to train the generated representations, avoiding the magnification of inter-domain discrepancies. The FocalNCE loss assigns higher penalties to negatives from the same domain as the query, strengthening domain-invariant alignment. Experiments show statistically significant gains across all metrics on four datasets.

The paper introduces FedTVD, a novel federated learning algorithm that weights client contributions using Total Variation Distance (TVD) to measure label distribution divergence, combined with dataset size, to mitigate the impact of label distribution skewness. Experiments show it outperforms state-of-the-art methods on FMNIST, CIFAR-10, and CIFAR-100, achieving up to 10.6% improvement over FedAvg on CIFAR-10 under highly skewed data. This work addresses a critical challenge in federated learning: data heterogeneity, particularly label distribution skewness, which can lead to biased models and poor convergence. By providing a simple yet effective weighting mechanism, FedTVD could improve the robustness and generalization of federated models in real-world applications where client data is often non-IID. FedTVD integrates Total Variation Distance (TVD) to measure the divergence between each client's local label distribution and a uniform global distribution, assigning lower weights to clients with highly skewed distributions. It also incorporates dataset size to ensure scalability and fairness, creating a dual-weighting mechanism that mitigates data imbalance.

## [C2L-Net: Fast and Accurate SOC Estimation with 20-Second Data Window](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.08653) ⭐️ 6.0/10

C2L-Net, a novel context-to-latest framework, estimates lithium-ion battery state-of-charge using only a 20-second historical window, achieving up to 60 times faster inference with fewer parameters than recent baselines. This addresses the computational cost and positional bias of long-history models, enabling more efficient and accurate SOC estimation for real-time battery management systems, which is critical for electric vehicles and grid storage. The model uses chunk-based feature extraction with Theta Attention Pooling and Fourier-based Seasonality Basis, a causal context encoder with GRU and Causal Cosine Attention, and a latest-measurement decoder inspired by recursive filtering. Experiments on a public drive-cycle dataset under multiple fixed temperatures show state-of-the-art or competitive accuracy with robust performance on unseen driving profiles.

## [ConMem: Contribution-Aware Memory Framework Boosts LLM Inspection Accuracy](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28126) ⭐️ 6.0/10

ConMem, a contribution-aware memory framework for LLM-assisted equipment inspection, was introduced, achieving 76.0% QA accuracy on real-world steel-equipment inspection logs. It reduces input tokens by 88.2% and response time by 86.6% compared to naive 8K-context LLM baselines. This framework addresses a critical limitation in current RAG systems for industrial inspection, which treat historical logs as static corpora and fail to prioritize early risk signals. By selectively retaining high-value evidence, ConMem can improve early-risk screening and reduce computational costs, benefiting industries that rely on long-horizon equipment monitoring. ConMem segments inspection logs into functional evidence units, estimates each unit's contribution via Shapley-style estimation, and retains high-value evidence under a constrained memory budget. Ablation studies show that functional-role-aware segmentation and contribution-based valuation help prioritize weak degradation signals for targeted field inspection.

## [Leakage-Free and Recency-Aware Embeddings Boost Knowledge Tracing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.17092) ⭐️ 6.0/10

This paper introduces a MASK label to prevent label leakage in knowledge tracing models and adds Recency Encoding to capture the distance since the last occurrence of a knowledge concept. Experiments show consistent accuracy improvements across DKT, DKT+, AKT, and SAKT on multiple benchmarks. Label leakage can inflate performance estimates and mislead model development in educational AI. This work offers a simple, effective fix that also incorporates forgetting dynamics, potentially improving the reliability and accuracy of adaptive learning systems. The MASK label replaces ground-truth labels only when leakage could occur, inspired by masked language modeling like BERT. Recency Encoding outperforms traditional positional encodings and is efficient and widely applicable to existing KT models.

**Background**: Knowledge tracing (KT) predicts a student's future performance from their interaction sequence with learning content, often using knowledge concepts (KCs). ## [ATLASFusion: Robust Sparse BEV Fusion for Multi-View Pedestrian Tracking](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.08421) ⭐️ 6.0/10

ATLASFusion introduces a reliability-aware sparse BEV fusion framework with three techniques: sparse perspective transform, density-aware weighted aggregation, and per-view BEV supervision. It achieves 95.9% IDF1 on WildTrack and improves MODP from 75.0% to 89.2% on MultiViewX, with strong robustness under calibration noise and reduced resolution. This work addresses a key challenge in multi-view multi-object tracking (MVMOT) by improving the reliability of BEV feature fusion, which is critical for applications like surveillance and autonomous driving. The demonstrated robustness and minimal computational overhead make it a practical improvement over existing methods. The sparse perspective transform projects only valid feature points to avoid interpolation artifacts, while density-aware weighted aggregation assigns higher confidence to spatially reliable regions. Per-view BEV supervision trains each camera's BEV features independently before fusion, and the method maintains performance under high-magnitude calibration noise (40.1% MODA vs. 0.0% for TrackTacular) and half-resolution input (92.5% MODA, only 1.1% decrease).

## [LLM-Driven AutoML for Cross-Lingual Handwritten OCR](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.15509) ⭐️ 6.0/10

This paper introduces a closed-loop AutoML framework where GPT-5, GPT-4o, and Claude Sonnet 4 act as autonomous neural architecture designers for cross-lingual handwritten OCR. The framework achieved mean test accuracies above 93%, a best accuracy of 98.1%, and inference latency between 41 and 44 milliseconds across 270 experiments on Arabic, Persian, and English datasets. This work demonstrates that large language models can effectively serve as AutoML agents for neural architecture search, potentially reducing the need for manual architecture design and domain-specific preprocessing in OCR. It could enable scalable, script-adaptive, and reproducible handwriting recognition across languages, impacting fields like document digitization and historical manuscript analysis. The framework operates in a closed loop where each LLM independently generates, trains, evaluates, and iteratively refines architectures based on performance feedback. The models are lightweight and specialized, trained on GPUs with standard optimization techniques, leading to high performance and low inference latency.
